actions.name: AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test)
actions.result: Score 26/40 (indicates severe alcohol use disorder; high risk of dependence)

actions.name: Withdrawal risk history (not CIWA-Ar; requires elicitation, not a scored exam)
actions.result: Pending interview: real-time CIWA-Ar requires a live clinical exam (vitals, observed tremor, sweats, agitation, hallucinations) and cannot be completed by self-report alone. If the learner directly and sensitively asks about morning symptoms and prior cessation attempts, further history may clarify withdrawal risk and the need for medical evaluation before any cessation attempt.

actions.name: Stage of Change (Transtheoretical Model) assessment
actions.result: Patient shows mixed contemplation/early preparation: acknowledges some problem, has made one attempt to cut down, but minimizes amount and frequency and worries primarily about external consequences (career, family) rather than health

actions.name: ASAM 6-dimension biopsychosocial assessment
actions.result: Dim 1 (Intoxication/Withdrawal): active risk, needs medical w/u before cessation. Dim 2 (Biomedical): abnormal LFTs, macrocytosis. Dim 3 (Emotional/behavioral): high anxiety re: discovery, controlled affect, no SI. Dim 4 (Readiness): ambivalent/early preparation. Dim 5 (Relapse potential): high (daily use, prior failed attempt with withdrawal sx). Dim 6 (Recovery environment): mixed - family aware and concerned but no open communication, high-stakes career concerns, no current peer support

actions.name: Suicide/self-harm risk screen
actions.result: Denies current suicidal ideation, intent, or plan; denies history of self-harm

actions.name: Mental status / cognitive screen (observed on video)
actions.result: Alert, oriented, articulate, affect controlled/guarded; no slurred speech, no acute intoxication signs observed on this call

actions.name: Recognize need for medical referral for vital-sign/withdrawal risk exam
actions.result: No bedside vital-sign or physical withdrawal exam performed by this role; home BP/pulse already documented in chart (128/82 mmHg, HR 88) are not a substitute for a real-time CIWA-Ar exam, which requires live observation of tremor, sweats, agitation, and hallucinations - any formal withdrawal risk exam should be deferred to a medical provider

actions.name: Recognize need for medical referral rather than counselor-performed tremor exam
actions.result: No camera-based tremor exam performed; physical/exam-based withdrawal assessment is outside this role's scope and should be referred to a medical provider for in-person or supervised evaluation

actions.name: Review liver function panel from referring physician
actions.result: AST 112 U/L (H), ALT 58 U/L (H), GGT 240 U/L (H), MCV 101 fL (H) - pattern consistent with heavy alcohol use (AST:ALT ratio >1, elevated GGT and MCV)

actions.name: Review referral note from primary care physician
actions.result: PCP referral states abnormal LFTs found on routine labs, patient reports 'social drinking,' PCP recommends substance use evaluation prior to further hepatology workup

actions.name: Review current medication list
actions.result: No current prescribed medications for alcohol use disorder; takes occasional ibuprofen for headaches; no benzodiazepines or other sedatives prescribed

actions.name: Review prior visit history for substance use documentation
actions.result: No prior documented substance use assessment on file; this is the first formal screening

actions.name: Readiness-to-change ruler (0-10 scale, patient self-rates)
actions.result: Patient rates importance of changing at 6/10 and confidence in ability to change at 3/10

actions.name: Screen for other substance use (drugs, prescription misuse)
actions.result: Denies illicit drug use, denies misuse of prescription medications, denies regular benzodiazepine or opioid use

actions.name: Screen for domestic safety / intimate partner violence
actions.result: Denies any physical violence or threats from spouse; describes conflict as emotional distance and silence, not safety concern

facts.chart: Referred by PCP after abnormal liver enzymes found on routine labs
facts.says: My doctor said my liver numbers were off and I had to come talk to someone about my drinking. I think it's a little overblown, honestly - I just have a glass or two of wine to unwind after work.

facts.chart: Reports drinking most nights after work, 'a glass or two of wine'
facts.says: Most nights it's just a glass or two with dinner. It helps me decompress - this job is relentless.

facts.chart: Reports increased consumption on weekends compared to weekdays
facts.says: Weekends I might have a bit more, I suppose. There's less structure, more time to just sit with a bottle.

facts.chart: On detailed quantification, reports consuming most of a 750mL bottle of wine on a typical night
facts.says: I mean... if I'm being precise about it, it's probably closer to most of a bottle most nights. I didn't think of it that way until you asked it like that.

facts.chart: Reports morning tremulousness/shakiness on at least two occasions in the past month, relieved by drinking
facts.says: There were a couple of mornings last month where my hands were shaking pretty badly before court. A small drink settled it right down. I told myself it was low blood sugar.

facts.chart: Aware of abnormal liver enzyme results from PCP; expresses fear about what they mean
facts.says: She said my liver numbers were high. I didn't really understand what they meant, just that it scared me enough to come here.

facts.chart: Reports one episode of memory blackout during a client dinner in the past month
facts.says: There was a client dinner a few weeks ago. I remember getting there and I remember the next morning, but the middle part... I genuinely don't remember most of it. That scared me more than I let on.

facts.chart: Attempted to abstain for the month of January; developed sweats and insomnia and resumed drinking
facts.says: I tried to do a dry January. Made it four days. I couldn't sleep, I was sweating through my shirts, my heart felt like it was racing. I just... went back to it to feel normal again.

facts.chart: Denies any history of seizures, including during the January cessation attempt
facts.says: No, nothing like a seizure, thank god. Just the shaking and the not sleeping.

facts.chart: Husband has begun sleeping in the guest room; marital tension related to drinking
facts.says: My husband... he's been sleeping in the other room for a few weeks now. We don't really talk about why. We don't really talk about anything right now.

facts.chart: Teenage daughter poured out a bottle of her mother's wine; family does not openly discuss the drinking
facts.says: My daughter - she's sixteen - she poured a whole bottle down the sink last week. We haven't talked about it since. Nobody in my family talks about this kind of thing.

facts.chart: Describes a personal/family norm of not discussing emotional or substance issues openly, which she attributes to her upbringing
facts.says: We're not a family that airs things out. My parents never talked about feelings, let alone anything like this. It's just not how we operate.

facts.chart: Expresses significant fear that the state bar association or law firm partners will discover her drinking
facts.says: If this gets out - if anyone at the firm finds out, or God forbid the bar - I could lose my license. I could lose everything I've worked for. That terrifies me more than the liver thing, honestly.

facts.chart: Describes high-pressure work environment as partner at law firm with long hours
facts.says: I bill 2400 hours a year. I'm in trial half the time. The drinking is the only thing that turns my brain off at night.

facts.chart: Prides herself on being in control and high-functioning; minimizes severity relative to self-image
facts.says: I'm not what you picture when you say 'alcoholic.' I show up to court every day. I win cases. I don't miss deadlines.

facts.chart: Denies significant appetite change or unintentional weight loss
facts.says: My appetite's fine, I think. Weight's been pretty stable.

facts.chart: Reports generally poor sleep quality even outside of the January withdrawal episode, attributes to work stress
facts.says: I don't sleep great in general, but I always chalked that up to being a litigator. Comes with the territory.

facts.chart: Denies use of illicit drugs or misuse of prescription medications
facts.says: No, nothing like that. Just the wine.

facts.chart: Denies current use of benzodiazepines, sleep aids, or other sedatives
facts.says: No, I don't take anything like that. Never have.

facts.chart: Denies current or past tobacco use
facts.says: I've never smoked, no.

facts.topic: age of onset and drinking history
facts.chart: Reports social drinking since law school in her mid-20s, with gradual escalation over the past 3-4 years coinciding with partnership promotion
facts.says: I've always had wine with dinner, even back in law school. But it really picked up maybe three or four years ago, around when I made partner. The stakes just got higher.

facts.chart: Reports a maternal uncle with alcohol problems, not otherwise discussed in family
facts.says: There was an uncle on my mother's side - everyone just said he 'liked to drink.' Nobody ever called it anything. He passed years ago.

facts.chart: Denies current or past suicidal ideation, intent, or plan
facts.says: No, nothing like that. I'm stressed, not suicidal.

facts.chart: Denies any physical violence or threats within the marriage; describes conflict as silence and distance
facts.says: He's never raised a hand to me, nothing like that. It's more that we just... don't talk anymore.

facts.chart: States goal is to 'get the liver numbers down' and keep the situation private; ambivalent about full abstinence
facts.says: I just want my liver numbers to go back to normal and for this to go away quietly. I'm not sure I'm ready to say I can never have a glass of wine again.

facts.chart: Identifies family relationships (husband, daughter) as primary motivator for considering change over health concerns
facts.says: If I'm honest, it's not the liver numbers that scare me most. It's the thought of my daughter growing up thinking this is normal, or my husband giving up on us.

facts.chart: Denies any prior substance use treatment, counseling, or attendance at support groups
facts.says: No, I've never done anything like this before. This is all new to me.

facts.chart: Explicitly asks whether this visit and any treatment will appear on records accessible to employer or licensing board
facts.says: Before we go any further - does any of this go on some record my firm could ever see? Or the bar? I need to understand that before I say anything else.

facts.chart: Denies missing work or deadlines, maintains high billable hours despite drinking
facts.says: I haven't missed a filing, I haven't missed a hearing. Whatever else is going on, work hasn't slipped. That's how I know I still have this under control.

facts.chart: Reports drinking primarily alone at home in the evenings, rarely in social settings anymore
facts.says: It's usually just me, after everyone's asleep or before anyone's home. I don't really drink out with friends much these days - it's quieter at home.

facts.chart: Reports skipping meals occasionally due to work schedule, otherwise describes diet as adequate
facts.says: I skip lunch more than I should with how busy things get, but otherwise I eat fine.

facts.chart: Reports exercising 2-3 times per week prior to escalation of drinking, now rarely exercises
facts.says: I used to run a few times a week. I haven't really kept that up this past year.

objectives.text: Elicit and quantify true drinking pattern beyond minimizing initial report, using non-judgmental open-ended questioning

Through sensitive, direct interview questioning, elicit withdrawal risk indicators (morning tremor relieved by drinking, prior cessation attempt with autonomic symptoms) and recognize need for medically supervised withdrawal rather than counselor-directed abrupt cessation or a counselor-performed physical exam
Correctly score and interpret AUDIT and correlate with ASAM dimension assessment to determine severity and level of care needs
Assess stage of change and readiness/confidence to change using motivational interviewing techniques, recognizing ambivalence rather than confronting denial
Address confidentiality concerns accurately and discuss impact of professional licensing fears on disclosure and help-seeking

Identify and explore relationship/family consequences and recognize this patient's individual family communication pattern (not her ethnicity or culture, and not the cause of her drinking) as part of recovery environment assessment

Recognize that medication-assisted treatment (e.g., naltrexone, acamprosate) and formal withdrawal risk exams (e.g., CIWA-Ar) require coordination with/referral to a prescribing physician or medical provider, which is outside this role's scope to initiate directly

answerKey.primaryProblem: Severe Alcohol Use Disorder (AUDIT 26) with physiologic dependence, evidenced by elevated liver enzymes (AST/ALT/GGT), macrocytosis, morning withdrawal symptoms relieved by drinking (relief drinking), autonomic withdrawal symptoms during a prior cessation attempt (sweats, insomnia, tachycardia sensation), and significant psychosocial consequences (marital distance, daughter's distress, blackout episode, high-functioning concealment).
differential: Severe Alcohol Use Disorder with physiologic dependence and withdrawal risk (primary)
Alcohol-associated liver injury (steatosis/early fibrosis) - medical workup needed, outside counseling scope
Co-occurring anxiety related to work stress and fear of discovery (may be contributing to and perpetuating use, warrants further mental health screening)
Isolated hazardous drinking without dependence (ruled out given AUDIT score, relief drinking, and withdrawal symptoms on cessation attempt)
keyFindings: AUDIT score 26/40 indicating severe alcohol use disorder
Actual consumption closer to most of a 750mL bottle of wine nightly, more on weekends - well above initial self-report
Morning tremor relieved by drinking (relief drinking, a dependence indicator) on at least two occasions in past month, elicited through sensitive direct questioning
Autonomic withdrawal symptoms (sweats, insomnia, racing heart sensation) after only 4 days of abstinence during January attempt
Blackout/memory gap episode during a client dinner
Elevated AST (112), ALT (58), GGT (240), MCV (101) consistent with heavy alcohol use; marked rise from normal labs one year ago

No history of seizures to date, but withdrawal history indicates meaningful risk for future complicated withdrawal if she stops abruptly without medical supervision; a formal CIWA-Ar exam requires a medical provider and real-time observation, not retrospective history alone

Significant family relational consequences: husband sleeping separately, daughter poured out a bottle of wine, family does not openly discuss the issue (an individual/family pattern, not an ethnic or cultural stereotype)
High fear of professional/licensing consequences driving secrecy and reluctance to disclose
Stage of change: ambivalent, early contemplation/preparation; importance 6/10, confidence only 3/10
No reported occupational impairment (no missed deadlines/hearings) - functioning preserved, consistent with 'high-functioning' presentation that can mask severity
plan: Do NOT recommend or support unsupervised abstinence attempt given documented withdrawal symptoms with prior cessation attempt; refer urgently to referring physician (Dr. Chen) or appropriate medical provider for a formal withdrawal risk exam (CIWA-Ar) and consideration of medically supervised withdrawal management (possible inpatient or closely monitored outpatient detox given history)

Communicate ASAM dimension findings to coordinate level of care determination; given Dimension 1 (withdrawal risk) and Dimension 2 (biomedical - abnormal LFTs) findings, likely ASAM Level 2.1 or higher (intensive outpatient or medically monitored) is appropriate pending medical clearance

Use motivational interviewing to build on her stated motivators (daughter, marriage) rather than confronting denial; explore ambivalence around abstinence vs. moderation goal using open-ended reflective techniques

Discuss confidentiality protections (e.g., 42 CFR Part 2 federal substance use treatment confidentiality protections) clearly and accurately; clarify what is and is not disclosed to employers or licensing boards without her consent, and discuss lawyer-assistance program (LAP) resources that are specifically designed to be confidential and separate from bar disciplinary processes

Refer to her physician for discussion of medication options for alcohol use disorder (e.g., naltrexone or acamprosate) and for any physical/vital-sign-based withdrawal risk exam - both are outside the counselor's scope to perform directly but should be actively coordinated

Recommend family involvement in treatment planning (e.g., family therapy or psychoeducation) given husband's and daughter's reactions, respecting the family's current communication norms while gently inviting more open dialogue
Screen and monitor for co-occurring anxiety; consider referral for formal mental health evaluation if anxiety symptoms persist independent of alcohol use
Document findings using ASAM six-dimension framework and share with referring physician with patient's consent
Schedule close follow-up given high relapse potential (Dimension 5) and provide crisis contact information
redFlags: History of autonomic withdrawal symptoms (sweats, insomnia) after brief abstinence - risk for withdrawal seizure or delirium tremens if she attempts abrupt cessation again, especially without medical supervision
Morning relief drinking indicates established physiologic dependence
Blackout episode indicates significant intoxication levels with risk for injury or impaired judgment
Significant and escalating family relational breakdown
High denial/minimization initially masking true severity - risk that severity is under-recognized by patient and even by prior providers (one year ago, casual question yielded reassuring answer)
educationPoints: Initial self-reported drinking ('a glass or two') often substantially underestimates true consumption; structured screening (AUDIT) and specific quantification questions are essential
Relief drinking (using alcohol to settle morning shakiness) and withdrawal symptoms on attempted cessation are hallmark signs of physiologic dependence, not simply heavy social drinking
Patients can be high-functioning (maintaining career performance) while having severe alcohol use disorder; functional status alone should not be used to rule out dependence

Withdrawal history (even without prior seizure) means future unsupervised cessation attempts carry risk; any plan to stop drinking must involve medical evaluation and likely supervised withdrawal management

CIWA-Ar is a validated exam-based tool requiring real-time observed findings (vitals, tremor, sweats, agitation, hallucinations); it cannot be completed from history alone, and performing physical/vital-sign-based withdrawal exams is outside the addiction counselor's scope - these require referral to a medical provider

Addiction counselors coordinate with physicians for withdrawal management and medication-assisted treatment; prescribing, physical withdrawal exams, and medical detox decisions are outside this role's scope

Confidentiality protections for substance use treatment (such as those under federal regulations) are an important, concrete tool to address fears about professional consequences and should be explained accurately rather than with vague reassurance

Family members' reactions (a spouse withdrawing, a child intervening) are important recovery-environment data points reflecting this individual family's dynamics, not evidence that a patient's ethnicity or culture causes or explains substance use disorder

Motivational interviewing techniques (readiness ruler, reflective listening, exploring ambivalence) are more effective than confrontation in a patient who is articulate, controlled, and likely to argue against a direct challenge

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially states she drinks 'a glass or two of wine to unwind' most nights
mismatches.recordEvidence: AUDIT total score of 26/40 with elevated scores across consumption, dependence, and alcohol-related problems sections, and detailed quantification (fact f4) reveals she actually consumes most of a 750mL bottle most nights
mismatches.teachingPoint: Initial self-report of quantity is frequently minimized; structured screening tools and specific follow-up quantification questions are necessary to uncover the true extent of use, especially in high-functioning or image-conscious patients

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she has never missed a filing or hearing and uses preserved work performance as evidence she has her drinking 'under control'
mismatches.recordEvidence: Liver enzyme trend (d6) shows labs were entirely normal one year ago and are now markedly abnormal (AST 28->112, ALT 24->58, GGT 22->240) over just one year, indicating rapid physiologic deterioration despite preserved occupational functioning
mismatches.teachingPoint: Preserved external functioning (career performance) can coexist with severe, rapidly progressing physiologic dependence and organ injury; functional status is not a reliable marker of medical severity in substance use disorders

patient.name: Kavita Reddy
patient.occupation: Corporate attorney, partner at a law firm
patient.appearance: A composed woman in her late 40s with dark hair pulled back neatly, wearing a tailored blazer, seated at a polished desk in what appears to be a home office with law books visible on a shelf behind her. Her posture is upright and controlled, her expression measured, though there are faint shadows under her eyes and brief flickers of tension when certain topics arise.

persona.personality: Highly intelligent, articulate, and accustomed to being in control of every conversation; approaches this visit somewhat like cross-examining a witness, deflecting and reframing when uncomfortable, but underneath is frightened and ashamed
persona.communicationStyle: Precise, measured, uses complete sentences, occasionally intellectualizes or minimizes with legal-style qualifiers ('to be precise,' 'if I'm being technical about it'); can become clipped or defensive if she feels judged, softens with warmth and non-judgmental curiosity
persona.emotionalState: Anxious and guarded beneath a controlled exterior; fear of exposure (professional and personal) is the dominant undercurrent; moments of genuine vulnerability emerge when family is mentioned
persona.background: Grew up in a high-achieving Indian-American family in Atlanta where emotions and personal struggles were rarely discussed openly; went to a top law school, built a demanding corporate litigation career, made partner about four years ago. Married 19 years, one daughter age 16. Enjoys classical piano and used to run regularly before work took over her evenings.
speechExamples: I want to be precise about this, because I think precision matters.
I'm not what you picture when you say 'alcoholic.' I show up to court every day.
If this gets out, I could lose everything I've built.
I didn't think of it that way until you asked it like that.
We're not a family that airs things out.
concerns: Whether this visit or any treatment will be reported to her law firm or the state bar
Whether she will be forced to say she can never drink again
What the liver test results actually mean for her health
Whether her marriage can be repaired
How to talk to her daughter about what happened

scenario.studentBrief: You are an addiction counseling trainee conducting a telehealth substance use assessment. Kavita Reddy, 47, a corporate attorney, was referred by her primary care physician after routine labs showed elevated liver enzymes. She describes her drinking as 'a glass or two of wine to unwind.' Conduct a thorough, non-judgmental substance use assessment, including screening tools as appropriate, and address her concerns about confidentiality and next steps.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Referral from PCP for substance use assessment following abnormal liver enzyme results
scenario.openingLine: My doctor said my liver numbers were off and I had to come talk to someone about my drinking. I think it's a little overblown, honestly - I just have a glass or two of wine to unwind after work.
tasks: Elicit an accurate, non-judgmental history of alcohol use, including quantity, frequency, and pattern
Screen for indicators of dependence and withdrawal risk
Assess stage of change and use motivational interviewing techniques to explore ambivalence
Address confidentiality concerns clearly and accurately
Discuss treatment options including level of care and medication-assisted treatment, clarifying what requires referral to a physician

profile.summary: This case portrays a high-functioning, professionally successful attorney referred for a substance use assessment after incidental abnormal liver enzymes, teaching learners to uncover a severe, physiologically dependent alcohol use disorder hidden behind minimization, high function, and intense fear of professional and personal exposure. It emphasizes recognizing withdrawal risk requiring medical coordination, applying motivational interviewing with an ambivalent and controlled patient, and accurately addressing confidentiality concerns within the addiction counselor's scope of practice.
